items.title: 60499_Garvin Bushell oral history interview
items.q: I got some other musicians and I replaced them with a drummer -- had a good drummer there, and also a piano player, Gene Gilbo, who was piano player with the Trainiers, from California. Most of them were stationed here. He'd been with them for 25 years. He joined me and we went into a club

ctx.x: oboe player they didn't have. So, whenever an act came there that they needed a piccolo or oboe or bassoon, why I would go to the various hotels. So I did that for another couple years or so. And I met a trumbone player who was a jazz man from L.A., but he was making his living down there selling encyclopedias. Got rich. And also was a good jazz man. He couldn't read music but he could play. Very big guy -- Bob Smiten. So he introduced me to another fellow who I found out later on was president of Williams…

And sometimes I'd make $150.00 a gig for myself. So, to me it was a good business. And I took on a few pupils too. Private teaching wasn't much because Puerto Ricans weren't in the habit of paying $10.00 a lesson or something.. They could go to the conservatory for a whole season for -- whole semester for $25.00 -- all year. Attend the conservatory -- $25.00. That's all it cost. Government subsidizes the rest of it, I think, through the Ford Foundation and some other benevolent society. And we kept on with this…

were there -- we were struggling hard to get them to come out. The weekends they would show up, but -- the owners of the club had the drinks and I got a percentage of the money -- 40 percent or something like -- 60 percent -- I got 60 percent. I'd still have to go to my pocket to help make the payroll every week. So, we stayed there long enough for somebody to hear about us. That somebody was Eastern Airlines and when the vice presidents had heard us and when they opened up their big hotel, the Saramar Beach,…
